title: Episode 120: John Quincy Adams and the Gag Rule: The Crusade for Free Speech
description:
After suffering a bitter, slanderous defeat to Andrew Jackson in the presidential election of eighteen twenty-eight, most observers believed John Quincy Adams's public career was finished. Instead, the sixty-three-year-old former chief executive made history: he ran for a seat in the United States House of Representatives representing his Massachusetts hometown of Quincy, becoming the only former president in American history to serve in the lower house.

For the next seventeen years, Adams served as the fearless moral conscience of Congress. In eighteen thirty-six, alarmed by a growing flood of anti-slavery petitions from citizens across the North, Southern congressmen passed the infamous 'Gag Rule'—a resolution that automatically tabled and buried any petition mentioning slavery without reading, printing, or debate. Adams recognized this not merely as a defense of human bondage, but as a fatal dagger plunged into the First Amendment right of petition.

Single-handedly, frail, trembling with age, but possessed of an iron will and devastating rhetorical mastery, Adams waged a ten-year guerrilla war against censorship. Defying violent shouting matches, multiple attempts to expel him, and hundreds of anonymous death threats, 'Old Man Eloquent' refused to be silenced until the gag rule was decisively repealed in December eighteen forty-four. Here is George with the dramatic story of the crusade that rescued American free speech.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we begin our exploration of America's sixth President, John Quincy Adams. While his single term in the White House was paralyzed by partisan gridlock, Adams's true heroic chapter unfolded after his presidency. Returning to Washington as a humble congressman, he waged a lonely, decade-long battle against Southern slaveholders who sought to silence American democracy itself. When Congress forbade any discussion of slavery, Adams stood in the well of the House and fought for the fundamental right of every citizen to petition their government. Here is George with the story of Old Man Eloquent.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: AN EX-PRESIDENT'S SECOND CALLING
In the spring of eighteen twenty-nine, John Quincy Adams departed Washington a broken, deeply disillusioned man. The son of founding father John Adams, he had spent his entire life in public service—serving as a teenage diplomatic secretary in Russia, minister to the Netherlands, Prussia, Russia, and Great Britain, the greatest Secretary of State in American history under James Monroe, and finally the nation's sixth President. But his presidency had been suffocated by vicious factional warfare, culminating in his crushing defeat by Andrew Jackson in eighteen twenty-eight. At age sixty-one, retiring to his family farm at Peacefield in Quincy, Massachusetts, Adams expected to live out his remaining days in quiet scholarly obscurity.
Yet retirement brought him neither tranquility nor purpose. Adams was a man consumed by a puritanical sense of duty. When local neighbors approached him in eighteen thirty, asking if he would consider running for a seat in the United States House of Representatives, his friends were horrified. In the nineteenth century, for an ex-president to descend from the majesty of the executive mansion to the chaotic rough-and-tumble of the House was considered a shocking loss of dignity. Adams dismissed their vanity with characteristic moral clarity. He declared: 'No person can be degraded by serving the people as a Representative in Congress. Nor, after having been honored with the highest trust in the gift of the nation, ought any man to refuse the lowest office if he can render service to his country.'
In November eighteen thirty, Adams was elected to Congress by a landslide. He would hold that seat for seventeen years, through nine successive congresses, until the day he died. And in the tumultuous halls of the Capitol, the aging statesman would find his greatest, most enduring battlefield.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GREAT PETITION FLOOD
By the mid-eighteen-thirties, the American abolitionist movement was surging with evangelical fervor. Activists like William Lloyd Garrison, through his newspaper The Liberator, and the American Anti-Slavery Society mobilized thousands of ordinary citizens across New England, New York, and Ohio. Because the Constitution gave Congress exclusive legislative jurisdiction over the ten-mile square of the District of Columbia, abolitionists focused their energy on demanding the abolition of slavery and the slave trade within the nation's capital.
They wielded the most ancient, sacred weapon of Anglo-American constitutional liberty: the right of petition, guaranteed explicitly by the First Amendment of the Bill of Rights. Thousands of petitions poured into the House of Representatives. Many were signed by church congregations, Quaker societies, and notably by tens of thousands of women, who, lacking the right to vote, viewed the petition as their only voice in national governance. The rolls of parchment, covered in signatures and tied with black ribbon, arrived in sacks at the Capitol every morning.
Southern congressmen viewed these petitions with apocalyptic horror. To Southern plantation owners, slavery was not merely an economic institution; it was the foundation of their social order. They feared that even permitting debate on slavery in Congress would encourage enslaved people to rebel, destroy Southern property values, and pave the way for national emancipation. John C. Calhoun and his allies in the House declared that Congress had no right even to touch, read, or acknowledge petitions relating to human bondage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE GAG RULE OF 1836
On May twenty-sixth, eighteen thirty-six, Southern representatives, backed by Northern Democrats eager to protect party unity under Martin Van Buren, struck a devastating blow against democratic norms. Led by Representative Henry Laurens Pinckney of South Carolina, the House passed a fateful resolution: 'All petitions, memorials, resolutions, propositions, or papers, relating in any way, or to any extent whatever, to the subject of slavery, shall, without being either printed or referred, be laid upon the table, and that no further action whatever shall be had thereon.'
It was the infamous 'Gag Rule.' When the clerk called the roll for the vote, John Quincy Adams rose from his seat. While other members voted aye or nay, Adams defied the Speaker of the House, shouting through the chamber: 'I hold the resolution to be a direct violation of the Constitution of the United States, the rules of this House, and the rights of my constituents!' The Speaker pounded his gavel, ordering Adams to be seated, but the gauntlet had been thrown.
Adams was not an abolitionist firebrand in the mold of Garrison. He was a conservative constitutionalist who believed in gradual, legal reform. But to Adams, the Gag Rule was an intolerable outrage. It linked the preservation of slavery directly to the destruction of white civil liberties. If Southern slaveholders could strip Northern citizens of their constitutional right to petition their representatives, then the entire edifice of American republican government was hollow. Adams made a solemn vow: so long as he drew breath, he would force Congress to hear the cries of the people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: PARLIAMENTARY GUERRILLA WARFARE
Every Monday in the House was 'petition day,' when members from each state were called in turn to present memorials from their constituents. For the next eight years, Monday mornings became a masterclass in parliamentary guerrilla warfare, with John Quincy Adams as the solitary general.
Standing barely five feet seven inches tall, with watery eyes, trembling hands, and a voice that cracked with high-pitched age, Adams seemed frail. But the moment he spoke, he commanded the room with razor-sharp intellect, vast memory, and unmatched mastery of House procedure. He arrived with towering stacks of petitions. As the Speaker called Massachusetts, Adams would rise and calmly begin: 'I hold in my hand a petition from fifty-three ladies of Weymouth praying for the abolition of the slave trade...'
Instantly, Southern members would leap to their feet, shouting, 'Order! Order! Lay it on the table! Silence him!' Gavel blows rained down on the rostrum. Adams would stand motionless, wait for the shouting to subside, and then continue with relentless precision: '...praying for the abolition of the interstate slave trade, which I move be referred to the Committee on the District of Columbia.'
When the Speaker ruled the petition barred under the Gag Rule, Adams would smile faintly and pull another parchment from his desk: 'I hold another petition, Mr. Speaker, from three hundred citizens of Franklin County, which does not mention slavery, but prays that the Gag Rule itself be expunged as unconstitutional.' When that was silenced, he would introduce petitions from peace societies, petitions from free Black citizens, and petitions signed by schoolteachers. Adams turned every petition into an agonizing constitutional trial for the House leadership, exposing the hypocrisy of the Southern slaveocracy to the entire world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TRIAL OF OLD MAN ELOQUENT
In January eighteen forty-two, Adams's defiance brought the House to the brink of armed violence. On January twenty-fourth, Adams rose and presented a petition from forty-six citizens of Haverhill, Massachusetts. The petitioners, despairing of the Southern domination of the federal government, requested Congress to peacefully dissolve the Union rather than remain shackled to slavery. Adams stated that while he opposed disunion, the citizens possessed a sacred right under the Constitution to petition their government even for its own dissolution.
Southern fury detonated across the chamber. Members screamed that Adams was a traitor guilty of high treason. Thomas Marshall of Kentucky and Henry Wise of Virginia introduced sweeping resolutions to formally censure the seventy-four-year-old former President and expel him from the House in disgrace.
For nearly two weeks, the House was transformed into a national tribunal, with Adams standing alone in the dock defending his honor. Adams turned the tables with devastating fury. Speaking for hours each day, he systematically put the Southern slave power on trial. He cited the Declaration of Independence, the Virginia Bill of Rights, and the letters of Thomas Jefferson. He exposed the South's tyrannical censorship, its violence against postal carriers, and its assault on the Constitution. He pointed his finger directly at his accusers, reminding them that his father had helped birth the republic while their predecessors were still loyal to the British crown. One observer wrote that Adams 'stood like a lion at bay, tearing his persecutors to pieces.' Demoralized, exhausted, and utterly outmatched by Adams's legal genius, the Southern delegation finally threw up their hands and voted to lay the censure motion permanently on the table.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE REPEAL OF THE GAG RULE
By eighteen forty-four, the political tide was turning irrevocably. Through eight years of relentless crusading, Adams had transformed what began as a marginal abolitionist issue into a mainstream Northern crusade for democratic civil liberties. Northern voters, many of whom cared little for enslaved people, were outraged that their own elected representatives were being muzzled by wealthy Southern plantation owners. Northern congressmen who voted to uphold the Gag Rule were systematically defeated at the ballot box.
Every new session of Congress, Adams introduced a resolution to repeal the Twenty-First Rule, as the Gag Rule was officially numbered. Year after year, the margin of defeat narrowed: from forty votes, to twenty, to four. Finally, on the morning of December third, eighteen forty-four, on the opening day of the Twenty-Eighth Congress, John Quincy Adams rose from his desk once more. Without making a lengthy speech, he simply moved that the Twenty-First Rule be rescinded.
A Southern member moved to lay Adams's motion on the table, as they had done dozens of times before. But this time, the roll call told a different story. The motion to table failed, eighty-one to one hundred and four. Then came the vote on repeal. By a decisive vote of one hundred and eight to eighty, the House voted to abolish the Gag Rule forever. In his diary that evening, the old statesman wrote with profound, humble relief: 'Blessed, forever blessed, be the name of God!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: DEATH AT HIS POST: A STATESMAN'S IMMORTALITY
John Quincy Adams continued to serve in the House for three more years, fighting the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War, which he viewed as an unconstitutional conspiracy to expand slavery across the continent. Though his body was frail and he suffered a severe stroke in eighteen forty-six, his mind remained razor-sharp, earning him the affectionate, revered title of 'Old Man Eloquent.'
On the afternoon of February twenty-first, eighteen forty-eight, Adams was seated at his desk on the floor of the House. A resolution was introduced to decorate and reward generals who had served in the Mexican War. Adams, opposing the imperial conflict to the last, shouted an emphatic, booming 'No!' A few moments later, he reached for his desk, turned pale, and collapsed backward into the arms of the representative beside him. He had suffered a massive, fatal cerebral hemorrhage.
Business in the House halted instantly. The fallen statesman was carried gently into the Speaker's room just off the chamber floor, where a cot was prepared. He lingered for two days, drifting in and out of consciousness. His final recorded words, whispered to his colleagues gathered around his bedside, were: 'This is the last of earth. I am content.'
John Quincy Adams died in the Capitol building where he had waged his greatest battles. He proved to a skeptical world that an ex-president's greatest service need not end with the White House. By championing the right of petition and standing firm against the tyranny of censorship, he kept the flame of American liberty burning brightly in its darkest hour.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
John Quincy Adams's crusade against the Gag Rule proved that one principled statesman, armed with the Constitution and an unwavering moral compass, can stand down an entire political establishment. Next week, we look at Adams's other monumental post-presidential triumph: the legal battle of the Amistad, where the seventy-three-year-old former President walked into the Supreme Court to argue for the freedom of African captives who had fought their way out of slavery. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
